elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the work as a 'living systematic review and meta-analyses', identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective/review question: to compare pregnancy and neonatal outcomes between pandemic and pre-pandemic periods.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed and Embase databases, reference lists of articles published up until August 14, 2021 and included English language studies that compared outcomes between the COVID-­ 19 pandemic time period and the pre-­ pandemic time periods.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main inclusion criteria (English-language studies comparing pandemic vs pre-pandemic periods) but does not explicitly state the main exclusion criteria in the abstract.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed and Embase databases, reference lists of articles published up until August 14, 2021
elements.reason: The abstract identifies information sources (PubMed, Embase, reference lists) and reports the date through which they were searched (up until August 14, 2021).

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-­ Ottawa scale.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess risk of bias (Newcastle-Ottawa scale).

elements.quote: We conducted random-­ effects meta-­ analysis using the inverse variance method.
elements.reason: The abstract states the synthesis method (random-effects meta-analysis using inverse variance).

elements.quote: Forty-­ five studies with low-­ to-­ moderate risk of bias, reporting on 1 843 665 pregnancies during the pandemic period and 23 564 552 pregnancies during the pre-­ pandemic period, were included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and summarizes study risk-of-bias characteristics.

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB (35 studies, unadjusted odds ratio [uaOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-­ 0.98), but not in adjusted estimates (six studies, adjusted OR [aOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.80-­ 1.13). ... There was no difference in the odds of stillbirth between the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic time periods (24 studies, uaOR 1.11, 95% CI 0.97-­ 1.26 and four studies, aOR 1.06, 95% CI 0.81-­ 1.38). There was an increase in mean birthweight during the pandemic period compared with the pre-­ pandemic period (six studies, mean difference 17 g, 95% CI 7-­ 28 g).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes with numbers of studies, effect estimates, and confidence intervals for each outcome.

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB (35 studies, unadjusted odds ratio [uaOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-­ 0.98)...
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., uaOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-0.98).

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB (35 studies, unadjusted odds ratio [uaOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-­ 0.98)... This reduction was noted in studies from single centers/health areas (25 studies, uaOR 0.90, 95% CI 0.86-­ 0.96) but not in regional/national studies (10 studies, uaOR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-­ 1.02).
elements.reason: When comparing pandemic vs pre-pandemic groups the abstract indicates the direction of effect (reduction in PTB during the pandemic) and which group had lower rates.

The abstract does not provide a brief summary of important limitations (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations are discussed in the main text but are not summarized in the abstract.

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB ... There was no difference in the odds of stillbirth between the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic time periods. There was an increase in mean birthweight during the pandemic period compared with the pre-­ pandemic period (six studies, mean difference 17 g, 95% CI 7-­ 28 g).
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results (e.g., reduction in unadjusted PTB, no difference in stillbirth) conveying the implications of the findings.
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding for the review.
Although registration is reported elsewhere in the document (text_7), the abstract itself does not provide the registry name and registration number.

elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated (to conduct a living systematic review/meta-analyses comparing pandemic vs pre-pandemic pregnancy and neonatal outcomes), but it is not framed using a recognized question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO or a similar structured framework).

elements.quote: Studies were included if they compared pregnancy outcomes between the COVID-­ 19 pandemic period and pre-­ pandemic time periods and reported on any of the outcomes of interest. We excluded studies that only reported outcomes of pregnant women with COVID-­ 19.
elements.reason: This review addresses observational comparisons of time periods (pandemic vs pre-pandemic) rather than intervention effects; therefore specifying planned intervention comparisons via PICO is not applicable.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they compared pregnancy outcomes between the COVID-19 pandemic period and pre-pandemic time periods and reported on any of the outcomes of interest. We excluded studies that only reported outcomes of pregnant women with COVID-19. As we were interested in overall pregnancy outcomes, we did not restrict studies based on plurality (including both singleton and multiple pregnancies).
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study eligibility characteristics: comparison of pandemic vs pre-pandemic periods, required reporting of outcomes, exclusion of studies reporting only on pregnant women with COVID-19, and no restriction on plurality. It also states study designs were unrestricted ('any type of study design') elsewhere (text_8).

elements.quote: We searched PubMed and Embase databases, reference lists of included articles, and personal files for studies published up to August 14, 2021. The search strategy used a combination of the MeSH terms ... and included any type of study design published in the English language (Appendix S1).
elements.reason: The review specifies a date cutoff for included reports (published up to Aug 14, 2021) and a language restriction (English).

elements.quote: Full-text articles excluded, with reasons (n = 27) ... • No outcome data (n = 1)
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram (text_13/figure_6) explicitly lists 'No outcome data' as a reason for exclusion, distinguishing exclusion due to absence of measured outcomes from other reasons.

elements.quote: We planned for meta-analyses of studies that reported similar outcomes and were methodologically homogeneous. For binary outcomes, we calculated the summary unadjusted odds ratios (uaOR), adjusted OR (aOR) when available ... Post-hoc subgroup analyses were conducted for the two primary outcomes after dividing studies into single-center (or selected hospitals/centers in an area), regional (statewide or province-wide) or national in scope.
elements.reason: The manuscript defines the groups used in syntheses (by outcome and by study scope: single-center, regional, national) and links these subgroupings to planned/meta-analytic comparisons.

elements.quote: We excluded studies that only reported outcomes of pregnant women with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The authors provide a rationale for at least one notable restriction (excluding studies only of pregnant individuals infected with COVID-19) because the review aims to assess population-level pandemic impact rather than outcomes among infected individuals. However, other restrictions (e.g., English language) are stated without an explicit rationale, so rationale reporting is partial.

Khalil et al had overlapping data for stillbirth outcome with another study; however, preterm birth data were not overlapping, so only preterm birth data were used in this review. ... we extracted the data for Canada excluding Ontario from Liu et al. to avoid double counting of data.
elements.reason: The authors describe decision rules for selecting among multiple reports and resolving overlapping/inconsistent data (excluding a study from meta-analysis, selecting only non-overlapping outcomes, and excluding overlapping region data to avoid double counting).

elements.quote: The primary outcomes in this study were rates of PTB and stillbirth. Secondary outcomes included mean birthweight (continuous) and rates of low birthweight (LBW), spontaneous PTB, medically indicated PTB, and neonatal, perinatal, or maternal mortality. ... Outcomes were defined as follows: Preterm birth: Live births between 22 + 0 and 36 + 6 weeks of gestation were classified as PTB. ... Stillbirth: Death before the complete expulsion or extraction from the parturient of a product of human conception at or after 20 weeks of gestation. ... Birthweight: Infant weight in grams, measured as soon as possible after live birth. Birthweight < 2500 g was defined as LBW, birthweight < 1500 g was defined as very low birthweight (VLBW), and birthweight < 1000 gram was defined as extremely low birthweight (ELBW). Spontaneous PTB: Birth of a baby between 22 + 0 and 36 + 6 weeks of gestation following spontaneous preterm labor or preterm prelabor rupture of membranes. Medically indicated PTB: Preterm birth initiated by a healthcare provider for maternal or fetal indications. Neonatal mortality: Death of a newborn due to any cause before 28 days of age. Maternal mortality: Death of a woman either during pregnancy or childbirth from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management, or within 42 days of end of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists primary and secondary outcome domains and provides explicit definitions for each outcome domain (PTB, stillbirth, birthweight categories, spontaneous/medically indicated PTB, neonatal and maternal mortality).

elements.quote: Preterm birth: Live births between 22 + 0 and 36 + 6 weeks of gestation were classified as PTB. Data on PTB at < 28 weeks, < 32 weeks, and < 34 weeks of gestation were reported separately in some studies and were analyzed independently. ... Stillbirth: Death before the complete expulsion or extraction from the parturient of a product of human conception at or after 20 weeks of gestation. ... Neonatal mortality: Death of a newborn due to any cause before 28 days of age. Maternal mortality: Death of a woman either during pregnancy or childbirth from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management, or within 42 days of end of pregnancy.
elements.reason: Time frames/measurement windows are specified for the outcome domains (gestational age ranges for PTB and stillbirth, neonatal mortality <28 days, maternal mortality within 42 days), and some specific gestational cut-offs are noted.

elements.quote: Data on PTB at < 28 weeks, < 32 weeks, and < 34 weeks of gestation were reported separately in some studies and were analyzed independently. ... We contacted authors to obtain data on stillbirth and neonatal mortality when the outcomes were reported as 'intrauterine fetal death' and 'perinatal mortality'.
elements.reason: The authors state that they analyzed different PTB cut-offs separately and that they contacted authors to obtain comparable outcome data in some cases, indicating efforts to capture compatible results; however, there is no explicit statement that all compatible results (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought for each outcome domain or a comprehensive description of scope, so the reporting is partial.

elements.quote: For one study conducted in the Netherlands by Been et al, 54 data were presented using multiple cut-­ offs to define the pre-­ and post-­ pandemic periods, with several different comparisons, making it difficult to select one comparison that aligned well with the other studies; we, therefore, included this study in the systematic review but not in meta-­ analyses.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides at least one example describing why a study was excluded from meta-analyses because multiple, non-aligning comparisons complicated selection, with an explicit rationale. However, there is no overarching, systematic description of the process used to select among multiple compatible results across all studies, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: The outcomes of intrauterine fetal death and perinatal mortality, though specified in the protocol, were not included ultimately in the review (deviation from protocol).
elements.reason: The authors report a change from the protocol (certain protocol-specified outcomes were not ultimately included), which addresses a change in outcome-domain inclusion; however, the manuscript notes the deviation without providing a detailed rationale for why these specified outcomes were not included, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: For one study conducted in the Netherlands by Been et al, 54 data were presented using multiple cut-­ offs to define the pre-­ and post-­ pandemic periods, with several different comparisons, making it difficult to select one comparison that aligned well with the other studies; we, therefore, included this study in the systematic review but not in meta-­ analyses. ... As they reported Ontario data separately and for an overlapping period with Shah et al 49 , we extracted the data for Canada excluding Ontario from Liu et al. to avoid double counting of data.
elements.reason: The authors describe changes to selection processes (excluding a study from meta-analysis due to multiple non-aligning comparisons; excluding overlapping regional data to avoid double counting) and provide reasons for these decisions, fulfilling the requirement to report changes to processes for selecting results with rationales.

elements.quote: The primary outcomes in this study were rates of PTB and stillbirth. Secondary outcomes included mean birthweight (continuous) and rates of low birthweight (LBW), spontaneous PTB, medically indicated PTB, and neonatal, perinatal, or maternal mortality.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies primary outcomes (PTB and stillbirth) and lists secondary outcomes, indicating which outcomes were considered primary for interpretation, but it does not provide a detailed rationale explaining why these outcomes were prioritized over others, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: The information extracted included details of the publication, study setting and size, pre-­ pandemic period definition, pandemic period definition, and rates of the reported outcomes in pre-­ pandemic and pandemic time periods.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state the specific variables extracted (publication details, study setting and size, definitions of pre- and pandemic periods, and outcome rates). In addition, multiple tables (e.g., table_0, table_1, table_2, table_3) display and define other variables sought such as factors adjusted for, statistical approach, outcomes, neonatal characteristics, and population level.

No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is provided in the retrieved evidence. The text notes that the authors "relied only on published information," but does not describe assumptions or imputations for missing/unclear data.

elements.quote: Data from the eligible studies were independently extracted by two authors (JY and PS) using a predefined, standardized extraction form.
elements.reason: Although the methods state a predefined, standardized extraction form was used, no citation or reference for a tool or guidance used to determine which data items to collect is provided in the retrieved evidence (i.e., the extraction form is not cited or described further).

elements.quote: We anticipated that primarily observational studies would be in - cluded in this review, so we used the Newcastle-­ Ottawa Scale 15 for cohort studies to assess risk of bias.
elements.reason: The risk-of-bias tool (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies) is named, but no version or detailed citation/version information is provided.

elements.quote: This scale assesses risk of bias in the domains of selection, comparability, and outcomes, and assigns a maximum score of 9.
elements.reason: The domains/components assessed by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (selection, comparability, outcomes) and scoring approach are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Studies with scores of 0 to 3 were considered to have high risk of bias, those with scores of 4 to 6 had moderate risk of bias, and those with scores of 7 to 9 had low risk of bias.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement scheme and the score cut-offs used to derive overall judgments are reported.
No information is provided about any adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool.

elements.quote: we used the Newcastle-­ Ottawa Scale 15 for cohort studies to assess risk of bias.
elements.reason: The authors used an existing tool (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale); there is no indication they developed a new risk-of-bias tool, so this item does not apply.
The report does not state how many reviewers assessed risk of bias, whether they worked independently, or the procedures for resolving disagreements about risk-of-bias assessments.
No processes for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators are described in the provided evidence.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are mentioned in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: For binary outcomes, we calculated the summary unadjusted odds ratios (uaOR), adjusted OR (aOR) when available and 95% CI, whereas for birthweight we calculated the mean difference and 95% CI.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly specifies the effect measures used for outcomes: unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios for binary outcomes and mean difference for birthweight, with 95% CIs.
No evidence was found specifying thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect sizes (e.g., cutoffs for small/medium/large effects) or any rationale for such thresholds.
No description was found of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., converting odds ratios to risk ratios).
Although the effect measures used are stated, the manuscript does not provide a justification or rationale for the choice of those effect measures.

elements.quote: We planned for meta- analyses of studies that reported similar outcomes and were methodologically homogeneous. For binary outcomes, we calculated the summary unadjusted odds ratios (uaOR), adjusted OR (aOR) when available and 95% CI... We planned to meta- analyze adjusted estimates from studies that reported them, understanding that studies will have adjusted for different factors based on data availability and baseline differences.
elements.reason: The Methods explicitly state the planned process to decide which studies would be pooled in syntheses: only studies reporting similar outcomes and judged methodologically homogeneous would be meta-analyzed; adjusted estimates would be pooled when reported. Additional supporting text (text_8 and text_13) gives inclusion/exclusion criteria and examples of decisions (e.g., excluding a study from meta-analysis because its multiple comparisons could not be aligned), demonstrating how eligibility for each synthesis was determined.

elements.quote: For binary outcomes, we calculated the summary unadjusted odds ratios (uaOR), adjusted OR (aOR) when available and 95% CI, whereas for birthweight we calculated the mean difference and 95% CI. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q statistic and quantified by calculating the I 2 values. We expected clinical and methodological heterogeneity between studies, so planned a priori for random effect meta-analyses using the inverse variance method.
